Mr. S. K. Sinha, J.: Complainant is the petitioner who challenges the judgment and order dated 1.11.99 of the 'corned Sessions Judge Narail in Criminal Revision Nos. 14 of 1999 and 27 of 1999. Criminal Revision No. 14 of 1999 was preferred against the order dated 5.5.99 of the learned Magistrate in G.R. Case No. 117 of 1998 rejecting the naraji petition filed by the petitioner and accepting the police report submitted under Section 173(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure Criminal Revision No. 27 of 1999 was preferred against the order dated 26.6.99 of the learned Magistrate in M.P. Case No. 409 of 1998 rejecting the naraji petition against the dismissal of the complaint made by the petitioner. 

 2. Facts relevant for the disposal of this Rule is as follows: Petitioner made a complaint before the court of Magistrate, Narail against accused opposite parties on 31.8.98 alleging inter alia that on the date of occurrence on 15.5.98 at about 12.30 P.M. accused persons were returning with load of paddy in 9 vehicles. When they reached by the side of her house, they being armed with lethal weapons stood there for preventing any sort of attack by Akbor Sarder's people. At that time local police also appeared there and tried to seize the paddy. Accused Abu Taleb Mollah thought that the Jarip Molla's people came to prevent them he passed order to kill them. At one stage deceased Amirul Islam, husband of the complainant came there to dissuade the tussle when a piece of brick-bat struck on the chest of her husband who fell down on the ground. Thereafter Abu Taleb gave a lathi blow on the head of her husband and other accused persons also indiscriminately assaulted her husband. Soon thereafter her husband succumbed to the injuries and on getting the information of the death of her husband she became puzzled. Abu Taleb is inimical to her husband who caused the death of her husband and with a view divert the real incident, he lodged an F.I.R. implicating some persons being Narail P.S. Case No. 13 dated 15.5.98. After the incident Abu Taleb threatened her and her son not to disclose the real incident and out of fear of life of her son, she did not lodge any complaint earlier. After a bit improvement of the situation she instituted the complaint.

Jalaluddin completed the investigation and submitted charge sheet against 25 Perused persons under different sections including Section 302 of the Penal Code that after institution of the said case this present complaint was filed, that complainant 

 complainant filed a naraji petition. The learned Magistrate without passing any order on the naraji petition kept the same on 30.l1.98 for order upon perusal of the case record. Thereafter the learned Magistrate 1w node; dated 5.5.99 rejected the naraji petition on the ground that 

 police officer submitted the report on as investigation into the case after following procedures, that there is no ground for further investigation into the case and accordingly he rejected the naraji petition, accepted the charge sheet and discharged the accused persons against whom final report was submitted. 

 5. Against the said order of the learned Magistrate rejecting the naraji petition complainant filed another naraji petition. The learned Magistrate rejected the said naraji petition by order dated 21.6.99 stating that over the same incident G.R. Case No. 117 of 1998 was started and in the said case, complainant filed a naraji petition and an order for further investigation 

 was made and thereafter the charge sheet was accepted and that since over the same incident a police case is pending, Iwo cases cannot be proceeded with over the same incident. 

 7. In this case, over the murder of Amirul information lodged by Md. Abu Taleb Molla, Md. Ruhul Amin and 24 accused as the alleged murderers. Maksuda Begum complainant then instituted complaint giving her own version against Md. Abu Taleb Molla and 15 others of them, some accused are common. In this context, courts below were fallen in errors of the procedures to be adopted by the learned Magistrate in disposing of these cases. 

 8. The law does permit more than one criminal proceeding in respect of the same matter. There may be cross cases where each of the two opposite sides charges the other with the commission of offences in respect of the same incident or there may be different versions as to who committed the offences alleged put forward by other side. Every separate proceeding is to be decided on its own record and is not affected by the decision in other case as it is obvious that there is possibility of a conflict between decisions in proceedings in respect of the same matter. But it is established principle being followed that there should not be conflicting decisions with respect to the same incident. It is totally absured that in respect of the same incident different persons be convicted in different proceedings inconsistent with each other. 

 9. Prior to the amendment in chapter XVII of the Code of Criminal Procedure by the Law Reforms Ordinance, 1978. there were conflicting decisions regarding the procedure to be followed in such eventuality of two cases instituted over the same incident as to whether a joint trial of the two sets of accused or a separate trial to be held. A Single Bench of the Lahore High Court in Criminal Revision No. 774 of 1964 and Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 1029 of 1984 (following the cases of Ali and others Vs. The Crown, PLD 1954 Lab 183, and Noor Ahmed Vs The State, 16 DLR (SC) 233 held that a joint trial of the two sets of accused, in the circumstances, would be in contravention of the provisions of Section 239 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The views taken in those cases is that either the one set or the other may have been really guilty of the offence in question and they could not be said to have participated in the same transaction together. 

 10. The question then is what should be the procedure to be adopted by the Trial Judge in disposing of these two cases. Their Lordships of the Pakistan Supreme Court in the case of Nur Elahi Vs. Ch. Ikram-UI Haq and another. I 8DLR (SC) 474 have settled the point, as follows: 

 After considering all aspects of the matter, we hold that a fair procedure would be for the learned Trial Judge to take up the complaint case first for trial. During that case the learned Trial Judge may call the witnesses mentioned in the Police chalan, if they were not already examined on behalf of the complainant, as Court witnesses under Section 540A of the Criminal Procedure Code, so that they can be cross-examined by both the parties. This will enable the Court to have the whole relevant evidence included in one trial and a decision could be arrived at after a proper consideration of the entire material relied on by the parties. The accused persons would in addition obviously have the right to adduce defence evidence if they so choose if that trial results in a conviction, it will be for the Public Prosecutor to consider whether or not he should withdraw from the prosecution with (2) 1964 16 DLR SC 233-PLD 1904, SC 120, the permission of the Court, under Section 494 of the Code of Criminal Procedure in the police chalan case. It would be easy for him to lake such a decision after the whole evidence has been thrashed out in the first trial. If the first case ends in an acquittal he might still have to consider whether the Police version has not been so seriously damaged by what has been brought out in the first trial as to justify withdrawal of the prosecution. Otherwise the send trial would be allowed to proceed to its normal conclusion and the parties would have the advantage of utilizing the material placed on the record at the earlier trial by way of cross-examination of the relevant witnesses as permitted by law. 

 Another difficulty may arise in respect or conducting the case on behalf of the complainant in the first trial. Normally of course under the law the Public Prosecutor is to be in charge of the case even if the trial is hosed on a private complaint. The Public Prosecutor however, in the special circumstances of the case, could permit the complainant's Counsel to conduct the proceedings on his behalf under his directions. Alternatively and that may meet the situation more adequately. Government in the interest of justice could notify the complaint's Counsel as a special Public Prosecutor for the conduct of that case alone. This would ensure full justice to the complaint and he would not be left with arty sense of grievance. He is at present challenging the bonafides of the Police investigation. We therefore, allow the appeal and direct that the trials will now be taken up by the Trial Judge in accordance with the observations made above. 

 11. The principles and guidelines as formulated by in the above case have not been overruled by the Supreme Court of Pakistan. To our Knowledge, our Appellate Division also did not reconsider the said decision. There is therefore no reason to depart from the said principles. We are of the opinion that said principles should be followed in cases of similar nature. Sometimes sonic Courts ignore the said principles and did not follow the principles enunciated by the Supreme Court of Pakistan and did not send both the cases for trial as case has been done in the pre-sent case. We have noticed in large number of cases that the Magistrates are making conflicting orders in the similar eventuality. In order to remove the controversy the legislature has amended Chapter XVII of the Code of Criminal Procedure by the Law Reforms Ordinance 1978 and inserted Section 205D. Even after insertion of Section 205D, we have noticed in many cases that the Magistrates are not following the said pro-visions or fail to address the said provision in appropriate cases. Even Sessions Judges fail to apply said amended provision in appropriated cases. 

 2050(1) When in a case instituted otherwise then on a Police report (hereinafter referred to as a complaint case), it is made to appear to the Magistrate during the course of the inquiry or trial held by him that an investigation by the police is in progress in relation to the offence which is the subject-matter of the inquiry or trial held by him, the Magistrate shall stay the proceedings 

 on such report, cognizance of any offence is taken by the Magistrate against any persons who is an accused in the complaint case, the Magistrate shall inquire into or try together the complaint case and the case arising girl of the police report as If both the cases were instituted on a police 

 (3) If the police report does not relate to any accused in the complaint case or if the Magistrate does not take cognizance of any offence on the police report the shall proceed with the inquiry or trial which was stayed by him in accordance with provisions of this Code. A plain reading of this provision appears that when in a case instituted on a complaint it is made to appear before the Magistrate during the course of the enquiry or trial that an investigation by the police is in progress in relation for the offence which is the subject of the inquiry, held by him. the Magistrate shall stay the proceeding of the inquiry and call for a report on the matter from the office in charge conducting the investigation if the report is submitted under Section 173 basing upon which cogniyance of offence is taken by any Magistrate against any person who is accused in the complaint case, the Magistrate shall inquire or try both the cases as if both the cases were instituted on a police report. If, however, police report does not relate to any accused to a complaint case or if the Magistrate does not take cognizance of an offence on the police report, he shall proceed with the inquiry or trial which was stayed by him in accordance with the provision of the Code. This is the statutory obligation of the learned Magistrate to be followed by the learned Magistrate. 

 12. in this case, as observed cattier. Over the same incident of murder of Amirul a police case instituted by Md. Abu Taleb Molla was under investigation when complainant petitioner made a complaint against some accused including Md. Abu Taleb Molla but some of the accused are common. The learned Magistrate noticed the said fact of Police investigation was in progress in his order dated 30th August 1998 but without staying the proceedings in the complaint case as per provisions of sub-section (1) of Section 2051) and calling for a report on the matter from the police officer conducting the investigation sent the complaint to the police for inquiry and report. Therefore there is total violation of sub-section (1) of Section 205D. The learned Magistrate cannot send the complaint for inquiry before the submission of police report tinder Section 173(1) in the Police case. After submission of police report under sub-Section (1) of Section 173 if the learned Magistrate finds that accused in the Polka' case and complaint case arc saint:, he shall hold trial or inquiry of both the eases together but if he finds that the case is triable by the Additional District. Magistrate or the Court of Sessions, he shall send for trial to the appropriate court ii both the cases were instituted on a police report. Some of the accused persons are not common in both the cases and therefore, sub-section (2) of Section 205D is not applicable in this case. In the premises there cannot be a joint trial under sub-section 12) of Section 205D and separate trial is required to be held as per provisions laid down in sub-section (3) of Section 205D since police report does not relate to sonic or the accused in the complaint case. In this case, the learned Magistrate did not follow the procedures provided in Section 205D and on an erroneous view dismissed the complaint. We are of the opinion that the provisions con tattled in sub-section (3) of Section 205D are in consonance with the principles enunciated in the case of Nur Elahi. Therefore the trial court shall take up the complaint case first for trial. In course of trial, the trial Court may call for the witnesses mentioned in the police case as court's witnesses under Section 540 so that they can be cross-examined by both the parties. If the trial ended in a conviction will he for the learned Public Prosecutor to consider whether or not he should withdraw from the prosecution with the permission of the court under Section 498 in the police case. If, however, the trial is ended in acquittal, the court shall take up trial of the police case. 

 13. The complaint petition has been dismissed by the learned Magistrate and no cognizance was taken against the accused in the complaint case and therefore the learned Magistrate cannot send the case unless cognizance is taken and formalities are complied with. To meet the said eventuality. We direct the learned Magistrate to hold inquiry into the complaint as per provisions of sub-section (3) of Section 205D. For holding such inquiry while holding such inquiry the learned Magistrate shall keep in mind to the provision of the proviso to sub-Section (2A) of Section 202.which provides that if the Magistrate inquiring into the case under Section 202 finds that the offence complained of is triable exclusively by the Court of Sessions, he shall call upon the complainant to produce all his witnesses and examine them on oath and then to pass necessary orders. This case being a murder case is exclusively triable by the Court of Sessions and therefore the learned Magistrate after following the produces provided in the proviso to sub-section (2A) of Section 202, shall send the case record to the Court of Sessions. 

 14. In this case we have noticed that the learned Magistrate has rejected the naraji petitions without examining the complainant-petitioner. It is now settled that a naraji petition is a complaint in all practical purposes and therefore. as soon as the naraji petition is tiled, the learned Magistrate is required to examine the complainant on S.A. and if he finds a prima-facie case against the accused persons he may take cognizance against them and if he did not find a prima-facie case, he may send the complaint for inquiry, as observed earlier, for ascertaining the truth or falsehood of the complaint. In this case, we have noticed that the learned Magistrate on receipt of the naraji petition on 5.5.99 perused the case diary, case record and the police report and was of the opinion that the allegations made in the complaint are false and accepted the police report submitted under sub-Section (1) of Section 173. As against the acceptance of the police report she again filed another naraji petition which was also rejected without examining the complainant on 21.6.99 holding the similar view that police after a thorough investigation. submitted a police report and that there cannot be parallel proceedings over one incident. The said orders are not only contrary to Section 200 but also violative to Section 205D of the Code of Criminal Procedure. It is a murder case, exclusively triable by the Court of Sessions. Both the parties of the police case and the com-plaint case admitted that Amirul Islam was murdered on 15.5.98 and gave two different versions. It is the trial court who will decide which version is correct on examination of the witnesses and it is none of the business of the police officer or the learned Magistrate to decide that the complaint version is false or that it was instituted at the instance of accused in police ease or that complaint was made at a belated stage. The learned Magistrate failed to notice that deceased Aminul Islam is the husband of the complainant and therefore, she is not prosecuting the litigation and come to court with any profit motive. What else an aggrieved widow who has been wronged can say other than the real incident. She lost her husband. In the complaint petition she made specific allegations against the informant of the police case Abu Taleb who according to her is the assailant of her husband. Whether accused persons named in the police case are the real assailants of Aminul Islam or the accused persons named in the complaint ease are the assailants are matters which cannot be decided by the police or the Magistrate. These are matters to be decided by a competent court having prediction to try the case. In that view of the matter we are of the opinion that this is Magistrate has committed error of law in dismissing the complaint. Similarly the coined Sessions Judge has committed for into her error in maintaining the orders of the learned Magistrate. In the premises we find substance in this Rule. 

 15. In the result the Rule is made absolute. The orders elated 5.5.99 in G.R. Case No. 117 of 1998 and 21.6.99 in M.P. Case No. 409 of 1998 and that of the iii dated 1.11.99 of the learned Sessions Judge in Criminal Revision Nos. 14 of 1999 and 27 of 1999 are hereby quashed. We direct the learned Magistrate to proceed with the case in accordance with sub-section (3) of Section 205D of the Code of Criminal Procedure and to hold inquiry into the complaint as per provisions provided in the proviso to sub-section (2A) of Section 202 and thereafter to send the case record along with the record of G.R. Case No. 117 of 1998 to the learned Sessions Judge Naiad for trial. We further direct the trial court to hold trial of the cases in the light of the observation made above.
